title: Target Sums Using Each Item Once
statement:
You get a list items of positive integers, which may contain repeated values, and a positive integer target. Return every different combination of items whose sum is exactly target. Each position in the list may be used at most once, so a value can appear in a combination only as many times as it appears in items.

Two combinations holding the same values the same number of times are the same, even if they came from different positions. Return each combination once. The combinations may come in any order, and the numbers inside one may also be in any order. If nothing works, return an empty list.

examples.why: There are two 2s, so [1, 2, 4] can be built in two ways. It is listed once.
Six pairs of positions give 6, and they are all the same combination.
1 appears twice in the input, so it may appear twice in a combination. 2 + 2 is not allowed: there is only one 2.

hints: Ignore the repeated values for a moment. How is this different from the version where parts can be reused?
Each position is used once, so recurse with i + 1. Then deal with repeats exactly as in the power set with repeated numbers.
Sort. In the loop at one node, skip items[i] when i > start and items[i] == items[i − 1]. Break as soon as items[i] is bigger than what is left.

explain.intuition:
Use the same template again, combining two earlier changes. As in the reuse version, a node is an answer when the sum left is 0, and sorting lets the loop stop at the first item that does not fit. As in the power set with repeats, each position is used at most once, so children recurse with i + 1, and equal values are skipped among siblings.

Why skipping siblings is enough: after sorting, equal values sit together. At one node, choosing the first 2 or the second 2 as the next item leads to the same set of completions, so only the first is explored. One level deeper, the second 2 is still allowed, which builds combinations like [1, 1, 2] when the input has two 1s. The test i > start captures exactly that.
steps: go(start, left): if left === 0, record a copy of cur and return.
Loop i from start. If i > start and items[i] === items[i - 1], skip. If items[i] > left, break.
pitfalls: Dropping the duplicate skip. The first example then lists [1, 2, 4] twice.
Skipping with i > 0. The second 1 in [1, 1, 2] is then never taken.
Recursing with i instead of i + 1. That lets one item be reused and builds [2, 2] in the third example.

complexity.time: O(2ⁿ · n) in the worst case; the target bound and pruning keep it small

solutions.title: Every subset of positions, then remove repeats
solutions.idea: Try every bitmask of positions, keep those that hit the target, and remove repeats with a set of sorted keys. Fine for 15 items, hopeless for 100.

solutions.title: Sort, skip repeated siblings, stop when too big
solutions.idea: The backtracking template with start = i + 1, the sibling skip for equal values, and a break once an item exceeds what is left.

followups: Rewrite it with a (value, count) list: at each distinct value, choose how many copies to take. Which version is easier to prove correct?
Every combination must use exactly k items. What extra pruning becomes possible?
